verdicts.notes: I checked all 12 r1 cards (6 true, 6 false). Every source URL loads, is official and current (the MDN 2025 URL layout, and the Cascade 5 TR CR Snapshot of 13 January 2022), and supports its card. Key quotes: MDN Cascade Introduction gives the precedence table (UA normal < user normal < author normal < animations < author important < user important < UA important < transitions), plus \"Animations take precedence over normal values\" and \"Property values being set in a transition take precedence over all other values set, even those marked with !important\". These settle sr1-01, 03 and 04. MDN !important: \"Declarations marked as important in the user-agent style sheets override all important declarations in the user style sheets\" settles sr1-02. Cascade 5, Element-Attached Styles: \"declarations that are attached directly to an element (such as the contents of a style attribute) ... take precedence over declarations the same importance that are mapped via style rule\" settles sr1-05. MDN Property_value_processing: \"The computed value of a property is the value transferred from parent to child during inheritance\" settles sr1-06. Cascade 5: \"For the root element, which has no parent element, the inherited value is the initial value of the property\" settles sr1-07. MDN revert: \"the initial value for the display property is inline, whereas a normal user-agent stylesheet sets the default display value of <div>s to block\" settles sr1-09. MDN unset settles sr1-11. MDN all: \"resets all of an element's properties except unicode-bidi, direction, and CSS Custom Properties\" settles sr1-12. I found no wrong answers. Minor points that I did not flag: sr1-09's lead-in \"In ordinary block flow\" adds nothing and could be dropped. sr1-03's \"running\" is harmless (a paused animation also applies its values). sr1-12's \"unregistered\" qualifier is unnecessary but does not change the answer. Overlap check against the rest of the deck: sr1-08 (and its replacement) and sr4-04 (box-sizing not inherited) share the \"non-inherited property defaults to initial\" pattern on different properties, so they do not duplicate each other and stay within the two-false-per-template limit. sr1-02 and sr2-03 (important layer reversal) are separate facts. True/false statement length averages are 83.7 vs 88.0, within the 5-character rule.

- 02: MDN @layer: "A rule in utilities would be applied even if it has lower specificity than the rule in theme."

verdicts.notes: I checked all 12 r3 cards (6 true: 01, 04, 05, 07, 10, 12; 6 false: 02, 03, 06, 08, 09, 11). Average statement length is 79.0 for true and 77.2 for false. Every statement is 120 characters or less and every explanation 240 or less. The Selectors 4 TR (Working Draft, 22 January 2026), section 15, confirms these verbatim: the A/B/C counting, \"ignore the universal selector\", \":is(), :not(), or :has() ... replaced by the specificity of the most specific complex selector\", :nth-child() as \"one pseudo-class selector plus the specificity of the most specific complex selector in its selector list argument\" (its own example: :nth-child(even of li, .item) = (0,2,0)), :where() replaced by zero, and the column-by-column comparison. So cards 03, 05, 06, 08 and 07 are right. Card 01 is backed word for word by MDN Specificity: \"the selector [id=\"myContent\"] counts as an attribute selector for the purpose of determining the selector's specificity, even though it selects an ID.\" Card 02 is backed by MDN's TYPE column, which lists \"pseudo-elements like ::before\". MDN Nesting_and_specificity confirms card 09: \"The specificity of the & nesting selector is calculated using the largest specificity in the associated selector list\", with the #a, b example giving 1-0-0. Card 10 matches MDN: same weights mean the last declared wins, and specificity is compared within one origin, importance and layer. Minor, not flagged: card 04 cites Selectors 4, which never says outright that combinators add zero (only its examples show it, e.g. \"UL OL+LI /* a=0 b=0 c=3 */\"). MDN Specificity says it directly: \"Combinators, such as +, >, ~, \" \", and ||, ... don't add any value to the specificity weight\". That URL would be a slightly better source. No duplicates found against r1 (inheritance cards), r2 (bare selector and :scope weight in @scope, proximity vs specificity) or r11 (matching behaviour of :is, :where, :has, :nth-child of S and nesting). flagged.evidence: The card turns MDN's necessary condition into a sufficient one: an auto dimension is not enough on its own. CSS Box Sizing 4 (https://drafts.csswg.org/css-sizing-4/), aspect-ratio property table: "Applies to: all elements except inline boxes and internal ruby or table boxes". So on a non-replaced inline box (a span) with both sizes auto, the ratio has no effect. A second case: a flex item in a row container with a fixed width, height: auto and the default stretch alignment. Its cross size is the stretched line size (CSS Flexbox 1, align-self: stretch), so its ratio is ignored even though height is auto. An expert can name both cases, and both are non-replaced boxes with an auto dimension where the ratio does nothing. The explanation is also vague ("no automatic dimension to resolve").
flagged.problem: "A non-replaced box" with "at least one dimension auto" includes inline boxes and stretched flex or grid items, where aspect-ratio has no effect. An expert could defend False. The wording "preferred `aspect-ratio`" mixes the property with the spec term.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer stays True). Statement: "`aspect-ratio: 2 / 1` on an empty block `div` with `width: 300px` and `height: auto` gives it a 150px height." Explanation: "With one automatic dimension, the browser derives it from the other through the ratio: 300px / 2 = 150px. When width and height are both set to lengths, aspect-ratio has no effect on the box." Keep the URL https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/Properties/aspect-ratio.

I checked all 12 r11 cards (6 true, 6 false) against their MDN pages, all of which load and are current. For card 11 I also checked the CSS Nesting editor's draft (5 February 2026). Only one card is flagged; the other 11 pass.

The 11 cards that pass:
- **01, 02, 03 (combinators):** each matches its MDN definition. Child: "direct children of elements matched by the first". Next-sibling: "only if it _immediately_ follows the first element, and both are children of the same parent". Subsequent-sibling: "follow the first element (not necessarily immediately) and share the same parent element".
- **04 (:is() and :where() forgiving lists):** the :is page says "the incorrect or unsupported selector will be ignored and the others used".
- **06 (:has() styles the heading):** the :has page example `h1:has(+ p)` "applies the style to h1".
- **07 (:nth-child of S):** MDN says the of-selector picks "the nth element that matches that selector" and contrasts it with li.important:nth-child(-n + 3).
- **08, 10 (nesting without & and with & appended):** the Nesting/Using guide shows `.parent .child` for a nested selector without &, and `.bar &` parsing as `.bar .foo`.
- **09 (&:hover):** the Nesting_selector page shows `&:hover` parsing as `.parent-rule:hover`, which "applies to the parent element when hovered".

The current editor's draft says "&div is illegal, and must be written div& instead" and its changes note says "Switched &div back to being invalid". The Nesting/Using guide backs it more directly than the cited CSSNestedDeclarations page: "Declarations after nested rules are handled as CSSNestedDeclarations to preserve parsing order". The cited page is still acceptable.

Other checks:
- **Duplicates:** none. The r3 cards on combinator weight, :is(), :where(), nth-child-of and & test specificity, while r11 tests matching.
- **Templates and coverage:** no repeated false-statement template. Missing from the planned coverage: pseudo-elements and the double colon, :not() invalidated by a single bad selector, :has() parsing limits, @media nested in a style rule, and an invalid nested rule dropping only itself. I checked all 12 r13 cards: 6 true (03, 04, 06, 08, 11, 12) and 6 false (01, 02, 05, 07, 09, 10). Average statement length is 83.0 characters for true cards and 87.7 for false ones. With both replacements the true average becomes about 85.3, so it stays within the 5-character limit.

Verified correct, with quotes:
- 01: MDN hex-color describes the eight-value syntax #RRGGBBAA, with AA as the alpha component.
- 02: MDN rgb says of alpha: "If included, the value is preceded by a slash (/)". The legacy comma form appears in MDN's serialization note.
- 04, 05, 06: MDN oklch says L is the "perceived lightness", and "0% equals 0 and 100% equals 0.4". It also says hue angles differ: "in hsl() 0deg represents red ... in Oklab 0deg corresponds to magenta, while red is approximately 41deg".
- 07: Display P3 has different primaries and a wider gamut than sRGB (CSS Color 4 CRD, 7 October 2026, predefined spaces). The section supports the card only indirectly through its gamut-volume comparison and leaf example. The MDN color() page would be a more direct source, but this is not a failure.
- 08, 09: MDN color-mix gives "p1 = p2 = 50%" when both percentages are omitted. For p1 + p2 < 100% it normalizes them, and "an alpha multiplier of p1 + p2 is applied". So red 20% plus blue 20% in srgb gives alpha 0.4.
- 10, 11: MDN Using_relative_colors says "all origin color channel values resolve to appropriate <number> values". On alpha it says: "If the alpha channel value is not explicitly specified, it defaults to the alpha channel value of the origin-color". The page has no Baseline banner, as the prompt expects, and appliesTo Baseline 2024 is consistent with the compatibility data.

No duplicates: the only other color-related card in the deck is sr12-05 (prefers-color-scheme versus color-scheme), which tests a different fact. No card relies on gamut mapping, converted channel values, contrast, or the newer color-mix() forms.

The two flags are weak cards (a name giveaway in 12 and a definition card in 03). Each comes with a true replacement, so the balance is unchanged.

flagged.urlStatus: loads (W3C TR css-transitions-1, Working Draft 8 January 2026)
flagged.evidence: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/#starting: a transition starts only when "the before-change style is different from and transitionable with the after-change style". The answer (false) is correct, but the statement itself says the computed value "stays the same". A transition from X to X is visibly nothing, so anyone would answer False, and the card is a strawman. The fact the section wants is that computed values are compared, not declarations.
flagged.problem: Strawman. Its wording already gives away that nothing changes, so it does not test the computed-value comparison.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps false). Statement: "At a 16px font size, changing `width: 10em` to `width: 160px` starts a `transition: width 1s`." Explanation: "Transitions compare computed values. At a 16px font size, 10em computes to 160px, so the before-change and after-change widths are equal and no transition starts." Source stays https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transitions-1/#starting.

flagged.urlStatus: loads (MDN @starting-style, Baseline 2024, August 2024)
flagged.evidence: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Reference/At-rules/@starting-style: "used to define starting values for properties set on an element that you want to transition from when the element receives its first style update". The card is correct, but it says that @starting-style values are used as starting values. A player who knows nothing can read that answer from the at-rule's name.
flagged.problem: Name giveaway. The answer follows from the word "starting" in @starting-style.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps true) with the less obvious case MDN lists ("Elements changing to and from display: none"). Statement: "With a transition set, `@starting-style` supplies before-change values when an element's display changes from `none`." Explanation: "An element leaving display: none has no previous computed style, so its transitions would be skipped. @starting-style gives it before-change values, as it does for newly inserted elements." Same URL.

flagged.urlStatus: loads (MDN transform); the spec it relies on, https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transforms-2/#ctm, is a Working Draft dated 9 November 2021
flagged.evidence: MDN transform: "These properties are applied in the order: translate, rotate, scale, and finally transform." css-transforms-2 builds the matrix as identity, then "Translate by ... translate", "Rotate by ... rotate", "Scale by ... scale", then "Multiply by each of the transform functions in transform property from left to right". In that matrix product, the transform list acts on the element's points first (innermost) and translate acts last (outermost).
flagged.problem: "Applies ... before" has two readings. In MDN's written-order sense the answer is true. Geometrically, an expert can argue that the transform list is applied to the element first, which makes the answer false.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replace (keeps true). Statement: "`translate: 50px` with `transform: rotate(45deg)` renders like `transform: translate(50px) rotate(45deg)`." Explanation: "The browser composes translate, rotate and scale first, then multiplies in the transform list, so the individual properties act as if written to the left of the transform functions." Source: https://www.w3.org/TR/css-transforms-2/#ctm (or keep the MDN transform page).

verdicts.notes: Checked all 12 r14 cards in raw/css-fundamentals-b4.json (6 true: 05, 07, 08, 09, 10, 12; 6 false: 01, 02, 03, 04, 06, 11). All source URLs load and are current official pages. Quotes that settle the passing cards: 01, MDN animation: "the first value that can be parsed as a <time> is assigned to the animation-duration, and the second one is assigned to animation-delay". 03, MDN transition-behavior: "normal: Transitions will not be started on the element for discrete animated properties" (Baseline 2024, August 2024). 04, same page: "When animating display from none to block ... the value will flip to block at 0% of the animation duration". 06, MDN @starting-style: "The @starting-style at-rule and the 'original rule' have the same specificity ... If you specify the @starting-style at-rule before the 'original rule', the original styles will override the starting styles." 07, MDN @keyframes: "browsers will use the element's existing styles for the start/end states", and css-animations-1 says the browser constructs the keyframe from computed values. 08, MDN @keyframes: "Declarations in a keyframe qualified with the important flag set are ignored." 09, MDN @keyframes: "all keyframes in the @keyframes rule for that percentage are used for that frame. There is cascading within a @keyframes rule", and css-animations-1 says \"The rules within the @keyframes rule then cascade\". 10, MDN animation-fill-mode: forwards keeps \"the computed values set by the last keyframe encountered during execution\". 11, MDN animation-direction: alternate plays \"the first iteration being played forwards\". The 3 flags are 02 and 05 (weak_card) and 12 (ambiguous). Every replacement keeps the card's answer, so the section stays at 6 true and 6 false. No duplicates: registered custom properties as animatable values appear only in r10 (sr10-12), and r1 cards sr1-03 and sr1-04 test the cascade rank of animations and transitions, not r14 facts. One minor point that is not flagged: sr14-10 is close to readable from the keyword name \"forwards\", but it tests the core fill-mode behaviour and is acceptable at difficulty 1.

duplicates.why: Borderline duplicate. Both rest on one rule: !important reverses layer precedence, and Cascade 5 treats unlayered styles as an implicit final layer. Anyone who knows that the first declared layer wins for important declarations (sr2-03) can work out that layered important beats unlayered important (sr2-04). sr1-02 already teaches the same reversal at origin level. sr2-04 is the more surprising and more practical card, so keep it and replace sr2-03 with a true r2 fact that does not use the reversal, for example anonymous layers or nested layer dot notation.

conflictGroups.name: important-reversal
conflictGroups.why: sr1-02's explanation ('Important declarations reverse the ordinary origin order') and sr2-03's explanation ('The important flag reverses precedence among cascade layers') give away the same reversal that sr2-03 and sr2-04 test.

conflictGroups.name: origin-order-normal-vs-important
conflictGroups.why: sr1-02's explanation refers to 'the ordinary origin order' that important reverses, which tells the player that user important outranks author important while author normal outranks user normal. This answers sr1-01 (user normal over author normal, false). The two cards are the two sides of one origin-order distinction.

conflictGroups.name: scope-specificity-sides
conflictGroups.why: These are the two sides of one distinction: the scope root adds nothing to a bare selector, and an explicit :scope adds 0-1-0. sr2-10's explanation says ':scope contributes class-level weight when an author writes it explicitly', which implies the implicit case adds none (sr2-09). sr2-09's explanation likewise hints at sr2-10.

conflictGroups.name: scope-limit-boundary
conflictGroups.why: sr2-12's statement and explanation ('Scope boundaries constrain selector matching', 'descendants beyond its scope limit') frame the limit as the point where matching stops. That pushes the player toward the right answer for sr2-08 (the limit elements are excluded).

conflictGroups.name: proximity-vs-specificity
conflictGroups.why: sr3-11's 'Outside @scope, a closer ancestor ...' signals that closeness only matters inside @scope. sr2-11's explanation ('Proximity resolves competing declarations with equal specificity') tells the player that closeness never adds specificity, which answers sr3-11.

conflictGroups.name: max-argument-weight
conflictGroups.why: Both cards rest on one idea: the most specific argument sets the weight even when a lighter branch matches. sr3-06's explanation ('The ID's weight applies even when .item is the matching branch') and sr3-09's explanation ('takes the greatest specificity in the parent selector list') each give away the other. The two statements also share one false template: 'has class weight when the .x branch/parent matches'.

conflictGroups.name: zero-weight-selectors
conflictGroups.why: This is a near-mirrored pair from the same MDN sentence ('the universal selector and combinators add nothing'): 'universal adds 0-0-1' is false and 'child combinator contributes zero' is true. Seeing one strongly hints the other.

conflictGroups.name: percentage-vertical-reference
conflictGroups.why: This is a mirrored true/false pair worded almost the same way: 'Percentage padding-top uses the containing block's height' is false and 'top: 10% ... uses its containing block's height' is true. Either explanation sets up the contrast and makes the other card easy, or teaches the wrong generalisation if the two come close together.

conflictGroups.name: margin-collapse-arithmetic
conflictGroups.why: These are the two sides of one distinction (positive margins: the larger wins; mixed signs: the signed values are added). They are a mirrored pair: 'the larger margin sets their separation' is true and 'keeps the one with the larger absolute value' is false.

conflictGroups.name: containing-block-box
conflictGroups.why: Both statements say a box 'uses ... content box as its containing block' and both are false. sr6-04's explanation names the content box of the nearest block container for static boxes, and sr6-02's explanation names the padding box for absolute boxes, so each explanation sets up the contrast that answers the other card.

conflictGroups.name: stacking-context-z-auto
conflictGroups.why: sr6-12's statement 'isolation: isolate creates a stacking context ... even when its z-index is auto' implies that z-index: auto normally creates none. That gives away sr6-09 (relative plus z-index: auto creates one, false).

conflictGroups.name: nesting-ampersand
conflictGroups.why: sr11-08 says a nested selector without & means a descendant, and sr11-10's explanation says & stands for the parent selector itself. Together they answer sr11-09 (&:hover targets the card itself, not a descendant). sr11-08 and sr11-09 are a mirrored with-&/without-& pair.

conflictGroups.name: property-required-descriptors
conflictGroups.why: This is a mirrored template pair: '@property needs both syntax and inherits descriptors for a valid registration' is true and '@property with syntax "*" needs an initial-value descriptor for a valid registration' is false. sr10-09's explanation (initial-value optional for '*') and sr10-08's statement (only two required descriptors named) hint each other.

conflictGroups.name: container-query-ancestor
conflictGroups.why: sr12-09's explanation ('The name filters eligible ancestor containers ... selects the nearest eligible one') and sr12-11's explanation ('Descendants can query its custom property values') both say a query goes to an ancestor. That answers sr12-08 (an element never queries itself).

conflictGroups.name: oklch-vs-hsl
conflictGroups.why: sr13-04's explanation contrasts Oklch lightness with 'the HSL lightness parameter', which signals that Oklch and HSL channels are not the same. That gives away sr13-05 (the same hue mapping as hsl(), false).

conflictGroups.name: discrete-transitions
conflictGroups.why: sr14-03's explanation (only allow-discrete makes discrete properties transition) and sr14-04's statement (display flipping 'like other discrete values') interact. One teaches the discrete flip model and the other the opt-in, and in the same round each skews the other card's answer.

conflictGroups.name: starting-style
conflictGroups.why: sr14-06's statement and explanation take for granted that @starting-style supplies the starting values of an entry transition, which confirms sr14-05 (true).

conflictGroups.name: inherited-computed-value
conflictGroups.why: sr9-06's explanation ('keeps the number as its computed value. The child multiplies that inherited number') shows that inheritance passes the computed value, which answers sr1-06 (inheritance passes the used value, false).

conflictGroups.name: em-font-size-reference
conflictGroups.why: These three cards each ask which font-size an em or rem refers to, and sr9-02 and sr12-04 share one false template ('em ... uses the computed font-size of X'). Seeing sr9-03 (rem refers to the root) next to sr12-04 (em in a media query refers to the root's computed font-size) invites guessing by pattern instead of knowing the initial-value rule.

conflictGroups.name: non-inherited-property-template
conflictGroups.why: Both are false with the same template: 'a child's X follows its parent's X through inheritance', X being a non-inherited property (border-style, box-sizing). sr1-08's explanation ('does not inherit by default ... uses its initial value') primes the answer to sr4-04.

Explanations of false cards are 15 to 20 characters longer in r5, r6, r9 and r11, but the player sees them only after answering. Hedge and requirement words are balanced and rare: can 1T/1F, lets 1T/1F, needs 1T/1F, by default 1T/1F; must, every, only and always do not appear. Exploitable patterns:
(1) DIFFICULTY: 24 of the 28 difficulty-3 cards are false (86%). The only true hard cards are sr4-05, sr7-05, sr12-12 and sr14-12. The false hard cards are sr1-04, sr1-12, sr2-05, sr2-11, sr3-08, sr3-09, sr4-12, sr5-10, sr5-11, sr6-03, sr6-11, sr7-06, sr8-03, sr8-12, sr9-05, sr9-11, sr10-05, sr10-10, sr11-07, sr11-12, sr12-04, sr13-09, sr13-10 and sr14-06. In ten sections (r1, r2, r3, r5, r6, r8, r9, r10, r11, r13) both hard cards are false. If the UI shows difficulty or deals hard rounds, 'hard means false' wins almost every time. Difficulty 1 is 39T/31F and difficulty 2 is 41T/29F.
(2) The phrase 'as its containing block' appears 3 times, all false (0T): sr6-02, sr6-03, sr6-04.
(3) The 'restores an earlier/browser value' template appears 3 times, all false (0T), one more than the cap of two: sr1-09 ('restores the browser's block display'), sr2-05 ('restores an earlier declaration'), sr10-05 ('restores an earlier valid declaration').
(4) The equivalence template 'the same X as Y' or 'like Y' appears 3 times, all false: sr3-08 ('same specificity as .item'), sr13-05 ('same mapping ... as hsl()'), sr14-04 ('like other discrete values'). With sr10-01 ('names for the same custom property', false), equivalence claims are 4F against 2T (sr5-02, sr9-01).
(5) Concession clauses mark true cards: 'even when' or 'despite' appears 3 times, all true (0F): sr6-07, sr6-12, sr3-07.
(6) In specificity cards, every claim that something adds zero or keeps its weight is true (sr2-09, sr3-04, sr3-07). 'Guess zero' wins in r3.
(7) Some words lean toward false: 'valid' 5F/3T, and in r10 4F/2T (false: sr2-07, sr10-04, sr10-05, sr10-09, sr10-10; true: sr10-08, sr10-11, sr11-04). 'initial' appears in 5 false statements and 2 true ones (false: sr1-09, sr1-12, sr7-02, sr10-09, sr10-10; true: sr1-07, sr4-02).
(8) Some words lean toward true: 'inherit*' 8T/3F (false: sr1-06, sr1-08, sr4-04). 'keeps/preserves/retains/stays/remains' 10T/6F. 'gives' 5T/2F.
(9) Position-swap template 'the first X is the Y': 3 false cards (sr13-01 first hex pair is alpha, sr14-01 first time is the delay, sr14-11 first iteration is reversed) against 2 true (sr2-03, sr13-04). This is acceptable, but it is a recurring distractor shape.
(10) Mirrored statement pairs that let one card answer the other are listed under conflictGroups: sr4-06/sr6-05, sr5-08/sr5-11, sr10-08/sr10-09, sr3-03/sr3-04, sr11-08/sr11-09.
(11) The false template 'a child's non-inherited X inherits its parent's' is used twice (sr1-08, sr4-04), which is at the cap.
Side notes for the fact pass (outside this review's scope): sr1-10's explanation calls margin a property 'whose default behavior is to use its own value'; the accurate wording is that a non-inherited property takes its initial value. sr14-12 says the individual transforms are 'applied before' the transform list, which matches MDN's wording, but an expert could argue the opposite (geometrically, the transform list acts on the element first) and answer it either way.

source.title: CSS Flexible Box Layout Module Level 1

rewrite.reason: explanation_error: 'whose default behavior is to use its own value' is wrong. The new wording says the child receives the parent's computed value (MDN inherit: 'causes the element to take the computed value of the property from its parent element').
rewrite.statement: With `margin: inherit`, a child takes its parent's computed margin values.
rewrite.explanation: The inherit keyword makes an element take the computed value of a property from its parent. Margin is a non-inherited property, so this keyword is how a child copies it.

rewrite.reason: tell: breaks the 'restores an earlier/browser value' false template (3F, over the cap of 2) and removes the empty lead-in 'In ordinary block flow'. The fact and the answer (false) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: `display: initial` on a `div` gives it the browser's default `block` display.
rewrite.explanation: The initial display value is inline. In ordinary flow, display: revert instead rolls back author styling and recovers the browser's block value for a div.
rewrite.misconception: initial restores element-specific browser stylesheet values.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the Cascade 6 TR contains a note saying proximity applies 'regardless of specificity', which backs the opposite answer. MDN @scope says: 'Scoping proximity overrules source order but is itself overridden by other, higher-priority criteria such as importance, layers, and specificity.' The statement and explanation are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: Within one author layer, scope proximity takes precedence over selector specificity.
rewrite.explanation: The browser compares specificity before scope proximity. Proximity resolves competing declarations with equal specificity.
rewrite.misconception: A nearer scope root overcomes a more specific competing selector.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: the bare Cascade 5 root URL does not settle the card. MDN Specificity says it in one sentence: 'Styles for a directly targeted element will always take precedence over inherited styles, regardless of the specificity of the inherited rule.' The statement and explanation are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: A `p` color declaration beats a color inherited from a parent's ID rule.
rewrite.explanation: A declaration targeting the paragraph supplies its own color value. The parent's selector weight does not accompany an inherited value.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'a non-replaced box with one auto dimension' includes inline boxes and stretched flex items, where the ratio does nothing. The replacement is a concrete case that MDN confirms: 'At least one of the box's sizes needs to be automatic ... If neither the width nor height is an automatic size, then the provided aspect ratio has no effect'. MDN's own example uses a fixed width with height: auto.
rewrite.statement: `aspect-ratio: 2 / 1` on an empty block `div` with `width: 300px` and `height: auto` gives it a 150px height.
rewrite.explanation: With one automatic dimension, the browser derives it from the other through the ratio: 300px / 2 = 150px. When width and height are both set to lengths, aspect-ratio has no effect on the box.

rewrite.reason: explanation_error: a flex container is block-level but not a 'block box', because it is not a block container. MDN: 'When we use display: flex we create a block-level container, with flex children', and its table maps flex to block flex. The statement is unchanged.
rewrite.statement: `display: flex` gives an element a block-level outer display type in ordinary flow.
rewrite.explanation: The flex keyword equals the multi-keyword value block flex: the outer type block makes the container block-level in its parent's flow, while the inner type flex lays out its children.
rewrite.sourceTitle: Using the multi-keyword syntax with CSS display

rewrite.reason: tell: 'as its containing block' appeared only in false statements (sr6-02, sr6-03, sr6-04). This rewrite removes it here and also cleans up the awkward explanation. The fact (padding box, not content box) and the answer (false) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: An absolute child of a `position: relative` block is positioned against that parent's content box.
rewrite.explanation: An absolutely positioned box's containing block is the padding box of its nearest positioned ancestor, so its offsets are measured from inside the border, padding included.
rewrite.misconception: An absolute child's containing block excludes its positioned parent's padding.

rewrite.reason: tell: second removal of the false-only phrase 'as its containing block'. The fact (a transformed ancestor becomes the fixed box's containing block) and the answer (false) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: A fixed child of a block with `transform: translateX(10px)` is positioned relative to the viewport.
rewrite.explanation: The transformed block establishes the containing block for its fixed child, so the child is positioned relative to that block.
rewrite.misconception: Fixed positioning retains a viewport containing block inside a transformed ancestor.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'uses its nearest ancestor' did not say for what, and the natural 'containing block' reading is false. The new statement names the role. The verifier's text was not used as written because it had 'even when' (a concession tell) and 'without' (a negation). MDN position: 'a sticky element "sticks" to its nearest ancestor that has a "scrolling mechanism" (created when overflow is hidden, scroll, auto, or overlay), even if that ancestor isn't the nearest actually scrolling ancestor.'
rewrite.statement: A sticky box sticks to its nearest `overflow: hidden` ancestor when that ancestor has nothing to scroll.
rewrite.explanation: Sticky positioning attaches to the nearest ancestor with a scrolling mechanism (overflow hidden, scroll, auto or overlay), even if that ancestor never actually scrolls.

rewrite.reason: tell: concession clauses ('even when', 'despite') marked only true cards. This removes 'even when'. The fact and the answer (true) are unchanged.
rewrite.statement: `isolation: isolate` creates a stacking context for a block whose `z-index` is `auto`.
rewrite.explanation: The isolate value explicitly establishes a stacking context, independently of the block's z-index.

rewrite.reason: source_problem: Basic concepts does not state the auto-size, margin or min/max conditions. Flexbox 1 #align-items-property does: 'If the cross size property of the flex item computes to auto, and neither of the cross-axis margins are auto, the flex item is stretched ... while still respecting the constraints imposed by min-height/min-width/max-height/max-width.' The vague 'fixed margins' is replaced by a concrete row case. The verifier's 'no auto' wording was avoided because it is a negation.
rewrite.statement: By default, a row flex item with `height: auto` and zero margins stretches to its flex line's height.
rewrite.explanation: The initial align-items value is stretch: an item whose cross size computes to auto and whose cross-axis margins are not auto fills the line, within its min and max sizes.
rewrite.sourceTitle: CSS Flexible Box Layout Module Level 1

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: the card hinged on 0% versus 0, and the spec (flex-common: flex: <number> = <number> 1 0) has reverted 0% to 0. The card now tests zero versus auto, which holds under both MDN ('flex-basis is then equal to 0%'; flex: auto = 1 1 auto) and the spec.
rewrite.statement: `flex: 1` sets a flex item's flex-basis to zero instead of auto.
rewrite.explanation: A single unitless number sets flex-grow to that number, flex-shrink to 1 and flex-basis to zero (MDN writes 0%). The keyword flex: auto keeps the auto basis instead.

rewrite.reason: weak_card (near-copy of the MDN sentence). Rewritten instead of dropped: dropping all three weak r8 true cards would leave 3T/6F. MDN repeat(): auto-fit collapses empty repeated tracks after placement, and 'A collapsed track is treated as having a single fixed track sizing function of 0px, and the gutters on either side of it collapse'. The 1fr tracks then share the freed leftover space (flex_value: fr is 'a fraction of the leftover space').
rewrite.statement: With `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(100px, 1fr))`, two items in a wide container stretch across the full row.
rewrite.explanation: auto-fit collapses repeated tracks still empty after placement to 0px, along with their gutters, so the two filled 1fr tracks share the freed space.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: the current Houdini editor's draft makes all @property descriptors optional, so 'syntax and inherits required' could flip. Replaced with the stable scoped fact. MDN var(): 'If the custom property is registered with @property using a non-universal syntax and an initial-value, that initial value is substituted when no other declaration applies. The fallback is not used in that case.' 'Set nowhere' rules out a value inherited from a parent, and the wording avoids the verifier's 'without' (a negation).
rewrite.statement: For `--gap` registered as `<length>` with an initial-value and set nowhere, `var(--gap, 1rem)` returns that initial-value.
rewrite.explanation: A registered property with a non-universal syntax and an initial-value substitutes that initial value when no other declaration applies, so var() leaves the 1rem fallback unused.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'equivalent color values' over-generalised beyond the sRGB forms MDN shows. The new card uses MDN's exact case: 'other color values equivalent to sRGB blue (such as the hexadecimal code #0000ff) will match only if the --accent-color property was defined as a color with @property'. For unregistered properties, 'The match is essentially a comparison of the two values' tokens.' The statement was shortened to keep r12's true/false length gap under 5.

rewrite.reason: tell: breaks the false equivalence template 'the same X as ... in Y'. It also fixes r13's length tell: after the two true drops, true cards averaged 8.7 characters shorter than false ones, and the gap is now 4.0. The fact (oklch() and hsl() hue angles differ) and the answer (false) are unchanged. MDN oklch: 'The hue angles in oklch() are different from those in hsl().'
rewrite.statement: `oklch()` and `hsl()` assign the same hue to any given hue angle.
rewrite.explanation: Hue angles differ between color spaces: hsl() works in sRGB while oklch() works in Oklab, so the same angle can name a different hue in each function.
rewrite.misconception: oklch() hue angles map to the same hues as hsl() hue angles.

rewrite.reason: ambiguous: 'applies ... before' can be read in written order or in geometric order. The new statement is an equivalence that both readings agree on. css-transforms-2 #ctm: identity, translate by transform-origin, then translate, rotate, scale, then 'Multiply by each of the transform functions in transform property from left to right', then translate by the negated origin. So translate: 50px plus transform: rotate(45deg) equals transform: translate(50px) rotate(45deg).
rewrite.statement: `translate: 50px` with `transform: rotate(45deg)` renders like `transform: translate(50px) rotate(45deg)`.
rewrite.explanation: The browser composes translate, rotate and scale first, then multiplies in the transform list, so the individual properties act as if written to the left of the transform functions.

cards.statement: With `margin: inherit`, a child takes its parent's computed margin values.
cards.explanation: The inherit keyword makes an element take the computed value of a property from its parent. Margin is a non-inherited property, so this keyword is how a child copies it.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN inherit says the keyword gives the element its parent's computed value for any property, and MDN margin lists margin as non-inherited.

cards.statement: `display: initial` on a `div` gives it the browser's default `block` display.
cards.explanation: The initial display value is inline. In ordinary flow, display: revert instead rolls back author styling and recovers the browser's block value for a div.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN revert says the initial value of display is inline, while the user-agent stylesheet sets div to block. The prompt's cascade trap states the same.

cards.statement: Within one author layer, scope proximity takes precedence over selector specificity.
cards.explanation: The browser compares specificity before scope proximity. Proximity resolves competing declarations with equal specificity.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN @scope says proximity is overridden by importance, layers and specificity, and the prompt pins MDN over the 2024 Cascade 6 note.

cards.statement: A `p` color declaration beats a color inherited from a parent's ID rule.
cards.explanation: A declaration targeting the paragraph supplies its own color value. The parent's selector weight does not accompany an inherited value.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The anchor on MDN Specificity says directly targeted styles always beat inherited ones, whatever the specificity of the inherited rule.

cards.statement: `aspect-ratio: 2 / 1` on an empty block `div` with `width: 300px` and `height: auto` gives it a 150px height.
cards.explanation: With one automatic dimension, the browser derives it from the other through the ratio: 300px / 2 = 150px. When width and height are both set to lengths, aspect-ratio has no effect on the box.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN aspect-ratio says at least one size must be automatic, and its example uses a fixed width with height auto. Statement 109 chars, explanation 191.

cards.statement: `display: flex` gives an element a block-level outer display type in ordinary flow.
cards.explanation: The flex keyword equals the multi-keyword value block flex: the outer type block makes the container block-level in its parent's flow, while the inner type flex lays out its children.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN Multi-keyword syntax says display: flex creates a block-level container and maps flex to block flex.

cards.statement: An absolute child of a `position: relative` block is positioned against that parent's content box.
cards.explanation: An absolutely positioned box's containing block is the padding box of its nearest positioned ancestor, so its offsets are measured from inside the border, padding included.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN Containing block says that for absolute positioning, the containing block is the padding box edge of the nearest non-static ancestor.

cards.statement: A fixed child of a block with `transform: translateX(10px)` is positioned relative to the viewport.
cards.explanation: The transformed block establishes the containing block for its fixed child, so the child is positioned relative to that block.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN Containing block lists a transform other than none as forming the containing block for fixed elements, and the card uses transform, as the prompt requires.

cards.statement: A sticky box in an `overflow: hidden` ancestor with nothing to scroll sticks to that ancestor instead of the viewport.
cards.explanation: Sticky positioning attaches to the nearest ancestor with a scrolling mechanism (overflow hidden, scroll, auto or overlay), even if that ancestor never actually scrolls.
cards.reason: The wording lens was right that 'sticks to ... with nothing to scroll' is hard to picture, so the statement now names the visible result: the box does not stick to the scrolling viewport. I did not use its 'scroll container' fix. MDN overflow says an overflow: hidden box is a scroll container only 'if there is overflowing content', so with nothing to scroll that wording could be argued false. MDN position supports the new text: a sticky element sticks to its nearest ancestor with a scrolling mechanism 'even if that ancestor isn't the nearest actually scrolling ancestor'. Statement 118 chars. It uses 'instead of', with no negation or concession word.

cards.statement: `isolation: isolate` creates a stacking context for a block whose `z-index` is `auto`.
cards.explanation: The isolate value explicitly establishes a stacking context, independently of the block's z-index.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN isolation says that with isolate 'A new stacking context must be created.'

cards.statement: By default, a row flex item with `height: auto` and zero margins stretches to its flex line's height.
cards.explanation: The initial align-items value is stretch: an item whose cross size computes to auto and whose cross-axis margins are not auto fills the line, within its min and max sizes.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. Flexbox 1 #align-items-property states every condition: auto cross size, no auto cross margins, and min/max constraints.

cards.statement: `flex: 1` sets a flex item's flex-basis to zero instead of auto.
cards.explanation: A single unitless number sets flex-grow to that number, flex-shrink to 1 and flex-basis to zero (MDN writes 0%). The keyword flex: auto keeps the auto basis instead.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN flex expands flex: 1 to 1 1 0% and the spec gives 0, so 'zero' holds under both. flex: auto is 1 1 auto.

cards.statement: With `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(100px, 1fr))`, two items in a wide container stretch across the full row.
cards.explanation: auto-fit collapses repeated tracks still empty after placement to 0px, along with their gutters, so the two filled 1fr tracks share the freed space.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. MDN repeat() says auto-fit collapses empty repeated tracks to 0px and collapses their gutters. The wording lens's note about sr8-02 is context only and gives nothing away.

cards.statement: For an undeclared `--gap` registered as `<length>` with an initial-value, `var(--gap, 1rem)` returns that initial-value.
cards.explanation: A registered property with a non-universal syntax and an initial-value substitutes that initial value when no other declaration applies, so var() leaves the 1rem fallback unused.
cards.reason: Both lenses flagged the 122-character statement. I took the wording lens's 'undeclared' version, which is exactly 120 characters and also removes the awkward 'set nowhere', so it satisfies the fact lens's length fix too. I confirmed the fact on MDN var(): 'that initial value is substituted when no other declaration applies. The fallback is not used in that case.'

cards.explanation: Registering the property with <color> syntax lets style() treat equivalent values as a match, so blue, #00f and rgb(0 0 255) all match. Unregistered, the tokens are compared as written.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. This is the exact case on MDN Container size and style queries: #0000ff matches blue only when the property is registered as a color.

cards.statement: `oklch()` and `hsl()` share one hue wheel for their hue angles.
cards.explanation: Hue angles differ between color spaces: hsl() works in sRGB while oklch() works in Oklab, so the same angle can name a different hue in each function.
cards.reason: I merged the two fixes. The wording lens removed the absolute 'any given', but its own text kept part of the 'the same X as' template the editor was breaking. 'share one hue wheel' avoids both the absolute and the template. The fact and the answer are unchanged. MDN oklch(): 'The angles corresponding to particular hues differ across the sRGB (used by hsl() and hwb()) ... and Oklab (used by oklch()) color spaces.' Statement 63 chars, shorter than the editor's 65, so the r13 length gap does not widen.

cards.statement: `translate: 50px` with `transform: rotate(45deg)` renders like `transform: translate(50px) rotate(45deg)`.
cards.explanation: The browser composes translate, rotate and scale first, then multiplies in the transform list, so the individual properties act as if written to the left of the transform functions.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The css-transforms-2 #ctm steps apply translate, rotate and scale before the transform list (left to right), and the transform-origin translation wraps the whole product, so the two forms are equivalent.
